# Hilbert Space Direct Sum is Hilbert Space

## Statement

Let $\{H_i\}_{i \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of Hilbert spaces over the field
$\mathbb F \in \{\mathbb R, \mathbb C\}$, and let
$$H \;=\; \bigoplus_{i \in I} H_i$$
be their Hilbert space direct sum. Then $H$ is a Hilbert space.

## 0. Conventions and the definitions used

Throughout, $\mathbb F \in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ is fixed and every $H_i$ is a Hilbert
space over this same $\mathbb F$. We write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_i$ for the inner product
of $H_i$ and $\|\cdot\|_i$ for the induced norm $\|x\|_i = \sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle_i}$.
Inner products are taken to be linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second;
for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ conjugation is the identity and the two conventions coincide, and in
general the proof below is insensitive to the choice (interchange the roles of the two
arguments). We freely use the two standard facts valid in every inner product space: the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\langle x,y\rangle| \le \|x\|\,\|y\|$ and the triangle inequality
$\|x+y\| \le \|x\| + \|y\|$ (together with its consequence, the reverse triangle inequality
$\bigl|\,\|x\| - \|y\|\,\bigr| \le \|x-y\|$).

A **Hilbert space** is an inner product space over $\mathbb F$ that is complete with respect to
the metric $d(x,y) = \|x-y\|$ induced by its inner product.

**The direct sum.** Let $\prod_{i\in I} H_i$ denote the Cartesian product, i.e. the set of all
families $h = (h_i)_{i\in I}$ with $h_i \in H_i$ for each $i$. It is an $\mathbb F$-vector space
under the pointwise operations
$$(g + h)_i = g_i + h_i, \qquad (\lambda h)_i = \lambda h_i \qquad (\lambda\in\mathbb F),$$
with zero element $0 = (0_{H_i})_{i \in I}$; the vector space axioms hold because they hold
coordinatewise in each $H_i$. The **Hilbert space direct sum** is the subset
$$H \;=\; \bigoplus_{i\in I} H_i \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, h \in \prod_{i \in I} H_i \;:\; \sum_{i\in I} \|h_i\|_i^2 < \infty \,\Bigr\},$$
equipped with the operations inherited from $\prod_{i\in I}H_i$ and with
$$\langle g,h\rangle_H \;:=\; \sum_{i \in I} \langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i \qquad (g, h \in H).$$

Here $I$ is an arbitrary index set — possibly uncountable, possibly empty — so both sums above
are *unordered sums* over $I$. Section 1 fixes their meaning and records the facts we need; part
of what has to be proved is that the sum defining $\langle g,h\rangle_H$ converges for all
$g,h\in H$.

Accordingly, the proof of the theorem consists of the following four steps:

1. $H$ is a vector subspace of $\prod_{i\in I} H_i$ (Section 2);
2. $\langle g,h\rangle_H$ is a well-defined element of $\mathbb F$ for all $g,h\in H$ (Section 3);
3. $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_H$ is an inner product on $H$ (Section 4);
4. $H$ is complete in the induced norm (Section 5).

Section 6 contains two remarks, one on the degenerate case $I=\varnothing$ and one reconciling
the definition above with the alternative definition of $\bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i$ as a completion
of the algebraic direct sum.

## 1. Unordered sums

Let $\mathcal F(I)$ denote the set of all finite subsets of $I$. Ordered by inclusion,
$\mathcal F(I)$ is a directed set: it is nonempty ($\varnothing \in \mathcal F(I)$) and any two
elements $F, G$ have the upper bound $F \cup G \in \mathcal F(I)$.

**Definition 1.1 (sum of a nonnegative family).** For a family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ with
$a_i \in [0,\infty)$ put
$$\sum_{i\in I} a_i \;:=\; \sup\Bigl\{\, \sum_{i \in F} a_i \;:\; F \in \mathcal F(I) \,\Bigr\} \;\in\; [0,\infty] ,$$
the supremum of the finite partial sums (each of which is an unambiguously defined real number,
by commutativity and associativity of addition in $\mathbb R$). The family is *summable* if this
supremum is finite. For $F = \varnothing$ the partial sum is $0$, so the supremum is taken over a
nonempty set of reals and is $\ge 0$; for $I = \varnothing$ the value is $0$.

**Definition 1.2 (sum of a family in a normed space).** Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be a normed
$\mathbb F$-vector space and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a family in $X$. For $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ put
$S_F := \sum_{i\in F} x_i \in X$ (a finite sum; $S_\varnothing := 0$). We say $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ is
*summable with sum $s \in X$*, written $\sum_{i\in I} x_i = s$, if the net
$(S_F)_{F \in \mathcal F(I)}$ converges to $s$, i.e. if
$$\forall \epsilon > 0 \;\; \exists F_0 \in \mathcal F(I) \;\; \forall F \in \mathcal F(I): \quad F \supseteq F_0 \implies \|S_F - s\| < \epsilon .$$

*Uniqueness.* The sum in Definition 1.2 is unique when it exists: if $s$ and $s'$ are both sums,
then given $\epsilon>0$ choose $F_0, F_0'$ as in the definition and test with
$F = F_0\cup F_0' \in\mathcal F(I)$ to get $\|s-s'\| \le \|s - S_F\| + \|S_F - s'\| < 2\epsilon$;
since $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $s = s'$. Thus the notation $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ is unambiguous.

Definition 1.2 applies in particular to $X = \mathbb F$ and to $X=\mathbb R$ with the absolute
value; the next lemma shows that for nonnegative real families Definitions 1.1 and 1.2 agree, so
there is no conflict of notation.

**Lemma 1.3.** Let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $[0,\infty)$ and put
$M := \sup_{F \in \mathcal F(I)} \sum_{i\in F} a_i \in[0,\infty]$.
If $M < \infty$, then $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is summable in the sense of Definition 1.2 with sum $M$.
Conversely, if $(a_i)_{i \in I}$ is summable in the sense of Definition 1.2 with sum $s$, then
$M = s < \infty$.

*Proof.* Assume $M < \infty$ and let $\epsilon > 0$. By definition of supremum there is
$F_0 \in \mathcal F(I)$ with $\sum_{i\in F_0} a_i > M - \epsilon$. If $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ and
$F \supseteq F_0$ then, all $a_i$ being $\ge 0$,
$$M - \epsilon \;<\; \sum_{i \in F_0} a_i \;\le\; \sum_{i\in F} a_i \;\le\; M ,$$
whence $\bigl|\sum_{i\in F}a_i - M\bigr| < \epsilon$. Thus the net converges to $M$.

Conversely suppose the net converges to $s$. Apply Definition 1.2 with $\epsilon = 1$ to get
$F_0 \in \mathcal F(I)$ with $\sum_{i\in F}a_i < s+1$ for all finite $F \supseteq F_0$. For
arbitrary $G \in \mathcal F(I)$ put $F := G \cup F_0 \supseteq F_0$; then, since $a_i\ge0$,
$\sum_{i\in G} a_i \le \sum_{i \in F} a_i < s + 1$. Hence $M \le s+1 < \infty$, so by the first
part the net converges to $M$; by uniqueness of the limit, $M = s$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1.4 (Cauchy criterion: sufficiency).** Let $X$ be a **Banach** space and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$
a family in $X$ such that
$$\forall \epsilon > 0 \;\; \exists F_0 \in \mathcal F(I) \;\; \forall F \in \mathcal F(I): \quad F \cap F_0 = \varnothing \implies \Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F} x_i\Bigr\| < \epsilon . \tag{$\ast$}$$
Then $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ is summable.

*Proof.* First, the net $(S_F)_F$ is Cauchy in the following sense: for every $\epsilon>0$ there
is $F_0 \in \mathcal F(I)$ with
$$F, G \in\mathcal F(I),\; F \supseteq F_0,\; G \supseteq F_0 \implies \|S_F - S_G\| < 2\epsilon. $$
Indeed, take $F_0$ as in $(\ast)$ for this $\epsilon$ and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite.
Splitting each finite sum over the partition $F = (F\setminus G)\,\dot\cup\,(F\cap G)$,
respectively $G = (G\setminus F)\,\dot\cup\,(F\cap G)$, gives
$$S_F - S_G \;=\; \Bigl(\sum_{i\in F\setminus G} x_i + \sum_{i \in F\cap G} x_i\Bigr) - \Bigl(\sum_{i\in G\setminus F} x_i + \sum_{i \in F\cap G} x_i\Bigr) \;=\; \sum_{i \in F\setminus G} x_i \;-\; \sum_{i\in G\setminus F} x_i .$$
Both $F \setminus G$ and $G\setminus F$ are finite sets disjoint from $F_0$: an element of
$F\setminus G$ lying in $F_0$ would lie in $G$, because $F_0\subseteq G$, a contradiction; and
symmetrically. Hence by $(\ast)$ and the triangle inequality,
$\|S_F - S_G\| < \epsilon + \epsilon = 2\epsilon$.

Now for each integer $k \ge 1$ choose $E_k \in \mathcal F(I)$ such that $\|S_F - S_G\| < 1/k$
whenever $F,G \in\mathcal F(I)$ both contain $E_k$ (possible by the previous paragraph, applied
with $\epsilon := 1/(2k)$), and set $G_k := E_1 \cup \cdots \cup E_k \in \mathcal F(I)$. Then
$G_1 \subseteq G_2 \subseteq \cdots$, and since $G_k \supseteq E_k$ we still have
$$F, G \in\mathcal F(I),\; F \supseteq G_k,\; G \supseteq G_k \implies \|S_F - S_G\| < 1/k . \tag{1.1}$$
In particular, for $j \ge k$ we have $G_j \supseteq G_k$, so $\|S_{G_j} - S_{G_k}\| < 1/k$; thus
$(S_{G_k})_{k\ge 1}$ is a Cauchy *sequence* in $X$, and as $X$ is complete it converges to some
$s \in X$.

Finally fix $k \ge 1$ and let $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ with $F \supseteq G_k$. For every $j \ge k$,
applying (1.1) to $F$ and $G_j$ (both contain $G_k$),
$$\|S_F - s\| \le \|S_F - S_{G_j}\| + \|S_{G_j} - s\| < \tfrac1k + \|S_{G_j} - s\| .$$
Letting $j \to \infty$ gives $\|S_F - s\| \le 1/k$. Hence, given $\epsilon>0$, choosing an
integer $k > 1/\epsilon$ and $F_0 := G_k$ yields $\|S_F - s\| \le 1/k < \epsilon$ for all finite
$F \supseteq F_0$. Therefore $\sum_{i\in I} x_i = s$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1.5 (absolute summability implies summability).** Let $X$ be a Banach space and
$(x_i)_{i\in I}$ a family in $X$ with $M:=\sum_{i\in I} \|x_i\| < \infty$ (Definition 1.1). Then
$(x_i)_{i\in I}$ is summable and $\bigl\|\sum_{i\in I}x_i\bigr\| \le M$.

*Proof.* Let $\epsilon>0$ and choose $F_0 \in \mathcal F(I)$ with
$\sum_{i\in F_0}\|x_i\| > M - \epsilon$. If $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ is disjoint from $F_0$, then
$F \cup F_0$ is finite and
$$\sum_{i\in F_0}\|x_i\| + \sum_{i \in F}\|x_i\| \;=\; \sum_{i \in F\cup F_0}\|x_i\| \;\le\; M ,$$
so $\sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\| \le M - \sum_{i\in F_0}\|x_i\| < \epsilon$ and therefore, by the
triangle inequality, $\bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}x_i\bigr\| \le \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\| < \epsilon$. Thus
$(\ast)$ of Lemma 1.4 holds and $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ is summable; call its sum $s$. For the
estimate: given $\epsilon>0$ there is, by Definition 1.2, some $F\in\mathcal F(I)$ with
$\|S_F - s\| < \epsilon$, whence
$\|s\| \le \|S_F\| + \epsilon \le \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\| + \epsilon \le M + \epsilon$. As
$\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\|s\|\le M$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1.6 (linearity of the sum).** Let $X$ be a normed $\mathbb F$-vector space, let
$(x_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(y_i)_{i\in I}$ be summable families in $X$ with sums $s$ and $t$
respectively, and let $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb F$. Then $(\alpha x_i + \beta y_i)_{i\in I}$ is
summable with sum $\alpha s + \beta t$.

*Proof.* Let $\epsilon > 0$ and put $\delta := \epsilon/(1 + |\alpha| + |\beta|) > 0$. Choose
$F_1, F_2 \in \mathcal F(I)$ with $\bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}x_i - s\bigr\| < \delta$ for all finite
$F \supseteq F_1$, and $\bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}y_i - t\bigr\| < \delta$ for all finite
$F \supseteq F_2$. Put $F_0 := F_1 \cup F_2$. For finite $F \supseteq F_0$ we have, for finite
sums, $\sum_{i\in F}(\alpha x_i + \beta y_i) = \alpha\sum_{i\in F}x_i + \beta \sum_{i\in F}y_i$,
hence
$$\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}(\alpha x_i + \beta y_i) - (\alpha s + \beta t)\Bigr\| \le |\alpha|\,\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}x_i - s\Bigr\| + |\beta|\,\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}y_i - t\Bigr\| < (|\alpha|+|\beta|)\delta < \epsilon . \;\blacksquare$$

Note that the zero family $(0)_{i\in I}$ is summable with sum $0$; so Lemma 1.6 applied with
$(y_i) = (0)_{i\in I}$ and $\beta=0$ gives $\sum_{i\in I}\alpha x_i = \alpha\sum_{i\in I}x_i$.

**Lemma 1.7 (conjugation).** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a summable family in $\mathbb F$ with sum
$c$. Then $(\overline{c_i})_{i\in I}$ is summable with sum $\overline c$.

*Proof.* Complex conjugation is additive and satisfies $|\overline z| = |z|$, so for every
$F\in\mathcal F(I)$,
$\bigl|\sum_{i\in F}\overline{c_i} - \overline c\bigr| = \bigl|\,\overline{\textstyle\sum_{i\in F}c_i - c}\,\bigr| = \bigl|\sum_{i \in F}c_i - c\bigr|$.
The claim is now immediate from Definition 1.2. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1.8 (comparison and elementary algebra for nonnegative families).** Let
$(a_i)_{i\in I}, (b_i)_{i\in I}$ be families in $[0,\infty)$ and $\lambda\in[0,\infty)$. Then,
with sums as in Definition 1.1 and computed in $[0,\infty]$:

(i) if $a_i \le b_i$ for all $i$, then $\sum_{i\in I}a_i \le \sum_{i\in I}b_i$;

(ii) $\sum_{i\in I}(a_i + b_i) \le \sum_{i\in I}a_i + \sum_{i\in I}b_i$;

(iii) $\sum_{i \in I}\lambda a_i = \lambda \sum_{i\in I} a_i$ (with $0\cdot\infty := 0$).

*Proof.* (i) For each $F\in\mathcal F(I)$, $\sum_{i\in F}a_i \le \sum_{i\in F}b_i \le \sum_{i\in I}b_i$;
take the supremum over $F$. (ii) For each $F$,
$\sum_{i\in F}(a_i+b_i) = \sum_{i\in F}a_i + \sum_{i\in F}b_i \le \sum_{i\in I}a_i + \sum_{i\in I}b_i$;
take the supremum over $F$. (iii) $\sum_{i\in F}\lambda a_i = \lambda\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for each
$F$, and $\sup_F \lambda c_F = \lambda \sup_F c_F$ for $\lambda > 0$, while both sides are $0$
when $\lambda = 0$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 1.9.** For $x, y$ in an inner product space, $\|x+y\|^2 \le 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2$.

*Proof.* For real $a,b$, $0 \le (a-b)^2$ gives $(a+b)^2 \le 2a^2+2b^2$. Apply this with
$a=\|x\|,\,b=\|y\|$ and use the triangle inequality together with monotonicity of
$t\mapsto t^2$ on $[0,\infty)$:
$\|x+y\|^2 \le (\|x\| + \|y\|)^2 \le 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2$. $\blacksquare$

## 2. $H$ is a vector subspace of $\prod_{i\in I}H_i$

Write $P := \prod_{i\in I}H_i$, an $\mathbb F$-vector space as described in Section 0.

*$H$ contains $0$.* The family $0 = (0_{H_i})_{i\in I}$ satisfies $\|0_{H_i}\|_i^2 = 0$ for all
$i$, so all its partial sums vanish and $\sum_{i\in I}\|0_{H_i}\|_i^2 = 0 < \infty$. Hence
$0 \in H$, and in particular $H \ne \varnothing$.

*$H$ is closed under scalar multiplication.* Let $h\in H$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb F$. Then
$\|(\lambda h)_i\|_i^2 = \|\lambda h_i\|_i^2 = |\lambda|^2\|h_i\|_i^2$, so by Lemma 1.8(iii),
$$\sum_{i\in I}\|(\lambda h)_i\|_i^2 \;=\; |\lambda|^2\sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;<\; \infty ,$$
whence $\lambda h \in H$.

*$H$ is closed under addition.* Let $g, h \in H$. By Lemma 1.9,
$\|g_i+h_i\|_i^2 \le 2\|g_i\|_i^2 + 2\|h_i\|_i^2$ for every $i \in I$, so by Lemma 1.8(i),(ii),(iii),
$$\sum_{i\in I}\|(g+h)_i\|_i^2 \;\le\; 2\sum_{i\in I}\|g_i\|_i^2 + 2\sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;<\; \infty ,$$
whence $g + h \in H$.

Thus $H$ is a nonempty subset of $P$ closed under addition and under scalar multiplication, i.e.
a vector subspace of $P$; in particular $H$ is itself an $\mathbb F$-vector space under the
pointwise operations. Note also that $g - h = g + (-1)h \in H$ for $g,h\in H$.

## 3. The inner product is well defined

Let $g,h \in H$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $H_i$, and by $ab \le \tfrac12(a^2+b^2)$ for
real $a,b$ (again a restatement of $0\le(a-b)^2$),
$$\bigl|\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i\bigr| \;\le\; \|g_i\|_i\,\|h_i\|_i \;\le\; \tfrac12\bigl(\|g_i\|_i^2 + \|h_i\|_i^2\bigr) \qquad (i \in I).$$
Hence, by Lemma 1.8(i),(ii),(iii),
$$\sum_{i\in I}\bigl|\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i\bigr| \;\le\; \tfrac12\sum_{i\in I}\|g_i\|_i^2 + \tfrac12\sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;<\; \infty ,$$
the finiteness holding because $g,h \in H$. So the family
$\bigl(\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i\bigr)_{i\in I}$ is absolutely summable in $\mathbb F$. Since
$\mathbb F$ ($=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$) is a Banach space over itself, Lemma 1.5 shows that this
family is summable, and by the uniqueness of sums (Section 1) its sum is a uniquely determined
scalar. Therefore
$$\langle g,h\rangle_H \;=\; \sum_{i\in I}\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i$$
is a well-defined element of $\mathbb F$ for all $g,h \in H$.

## 4. $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_H$ is an inner product on $H$

Let $g, g', h \in H$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb F$. By Section 2 we have $g+g' \in H$ and
$\lambda g \in H$, and by Section 3 every inner product written below exists.

*Additivity in the first argument.* For each $i \in I$,
$\langle g_i + g'_i,\,h_i\rangle_i = \langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i + \langle g'_i,h_i\rangle_i$. The
families $(\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(\langle g'_i,h_i\rangle_i)_{i\in I}$ are
summable by Section 3, so Lemma 1.6 (with $X=\mathbb F$, $\alpha=\beta=1$) gives
$$\langle g+g',h\rangle_H = \sum_{i\in I}\bigl(\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i + \langle g'_i,h_i\rangle_i\bigr) = \langle g,h\rangle_H + \langle g',h\rangle_H .$$

*Homogeneity in the first argument.* For each $i$,
$\langle \lambda g_i, h_i\rangle_i = \lambda\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i$, so by Lemma 1.6 (in the
form noted after its proof),
$$\langle \lambda g,h\rangle_H = \sum_{i\in I}\lambda \langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i = \lambda\,\langle g,h\rangle_H .$$

*Conjugate symmetry.* For each $i$, $\langle h_i,g_i\rangle_i = \overline{\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i}$,
so Lemma 1.7 gives
$$\langle h,g\rangle_H = \sum_{i\in I}\overline{\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i} = \overline{\sum_{i\in I}\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i} = \overline{\langle g,h\rangle_H} .$$
(Combined with the two previous items, this yields conjugate-linearity in the second argument.)

*Positive definiteness.* Let $h \in H$. For each $i$, $\langle h_i,h_i\rangle_i = \|h_i\|_i^2 \ge 0$,
and $\sup_{F\in\mathcal F(I)}\sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 < \infty$ precisely because $h \in H$. By
Lemma 1.3 the sum of this nonnegative family in the sense of Definition 1.2 exists and equals
that supremum, so (using uniqueness of sums once more)
$$\langle h,h\rangle_H \;=\; \sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;=\; \sup_{F\in\mathcal F(I)}\;\sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;\in\; [0,\infty) . \tag{4.1}$$
In particular $\langle h,h\rangle_H \ge 0$. Suppose $\langle h,h\rangle_H = 0$. Since (4.1)
exhibits $\langle h,h\rangle_H$ as the supremum of a family of nonnegative reals, every partial
sum $\sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2$ is $0$; taking $F = \{j\}$ gives $\|h_j\|_j^2 = 0$, hence
$h_j = 0_{H_j}$, for every $j \in I$. Thus $h = 0$. Conversely, if $h=0$ then all partial sums
$\sum_{i\in F}\|0_{H_i}\|_i^2$ vanish, so $\langle 0,0\rangle_H = 0$.

Therefore $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_H$ is an inner product on the $\mathbb F$-vector space $H$,
so $H$ is an inner product space, with induced norm
$$\|h\|_H \;=\; \sqrt{\langle h,h\rangle_H} \;=\; \Bigl(\sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \tag{4.2}$$

Two consequences of (4.1)–(4.2) will be used in Section 5: for every $h\in H$ and every
$F \in \mathcal F(I)$,
$$\sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;\le\; \|h\|_H^2 , \tag{4.3}$$
and in particular, taking $F=\{j\}$,
$$\|h_j\|_j \;\le\; \|h\|_H \qquad (j \in I). \tag{4.4}$$

## 5. $H$ is complete

Let $(h^{(n)})_{n \in \mathbb N}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(H, \|\cdot\|_H)$, with
$h^{(n)} = (h^{(n)}_i)_{i\in I}$.

**Step 1 (coordinatewise limits).** Fix $j \in I$. For all $n,m$ we have
$h^{(n)} - h^{(m)} \in H$ by Section 2, and $(h^{(n)}-h^{(m)})_j = h^{(n)}_j - h^{(m)}_j$ by
definition of the pointwise operations; so (4.4) gives
$$\bigl\|h^{(n)}_j - h^{(m)}_j\bigr\|_j \;\le\; \bigl\|h^{(n)} - h^{(m)}\bigr\|_H \qquad (n,m \in \mathbb N).$$
Since $(h^{(n)})_n$ is Cauchy in $H$, it follows that $(h^{(n)}_j)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a Cauchy
sequence in $H_j$. As $H_j$ is a Hilbert space it is complete, so there is a (unique) $h_j \in H_j$
with $h^{(n)}_j \to h_j$ in $H_j$ as $n\to\infty$. Define
$$h := (h_j)_{j \in I} \in \prod_{i\in I}H_i ,$$
an element of the product that does not depend on any choice of $\epsilon$ below.

**Step 2 (uniform tail estimate).** *Claim:* for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is
$N = N(\epsilon) \in \mathbb N$ such that
$$\sum_{i\in I}\bigl\|h^{(n)}_i - h_i\bigr\|_i^2 \;\le\; \epsilon^2 \qquad \text{for all } n \ge N. \tag{5.1}$$

Indeed, let $\epsilon>0$. Since $(h^{(n)})_n$ is Cauchy in $H$, there is $N \in \mathbb N$ with
$\|h^{(n)} - h^{(m)}\|_H \le \epsilon$ for all $n,m\ge N$. Fix $n \ge N$ and
$F \in \mathcal F(I)$. For every $m \ge N$, applying (4.3) to $h^{(n)}-h^{(m)} \in H$,
$$\sum_{i\in F}\bigl\|h^{(n)}_i - h^{(m)}_i\bigr\|_i^2 \;\le\; \bigl\|h^{(n)}-h^{(m)}\bigr\|_H^2 \;\le\; \epsilon^2 .$$
The left-hand side is a sum of *finitely many* terms, and for each fixed $i$ we have
$h^{(m)}_i \to h_i$ in $H_i$ as $m \to \infty$, so by the reverse triangle inequality
$$\Bigl|\;\bigl\|h^{(n)}_i - h^{(m)}_i\bigr\|_i - \bigl\|h^{(n)}_i - h_i\bigr\|_i\;\Bigr| \;\le\; \bigl\|h_i - h^{(m)}_i\bigr\|_i \;\xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{}\; 0 ,$$
and therefore $\|h^{(n)}_i - h^{(m)}_i\|_i^2 \to \|h^{(n)}_i - h_i\|_i^2$ as $m\to\infty$ (the
square function is continuous). Letting $m\to\infty$ in the displayed inequality — legitimate,
as it involves a limit of a finite sum and a non-strict inequality — yields
$$\sum_{i \in F}\bigl\|h^{(n)}_i - h_i\bigr\|_i^2 \;\le\; \epsilon^2 .$$
Since $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ was arbitrary and $n\ge N$ was arbitrary, taking the supremum over
$F$ and recalling Definition 1.1 gives exactly (5.1). This proves the claim.

**Step 3 ($h \in H$).** Apply Step 2 with $\epsilon = 1$ and put $N_1 := N(1)$. Then the family
$h^{(N_1)} - h \in \prod_{i\in I}H_i$ satisfies
$\sum_{i\in I}\|h^{(N_1)}_i - h_i\|_i^2 \le 1 < \infty$, i.e. $h^{(N_1)} - h \in H$. Since
$h^{(N_1)} \in H$ and $H$ is a vector subspace of $\prod_{i\in I}H_i$ (Section 2),
$$h \;=\; h^{(N_1)} - \bigl(h^{(N_1)} - h\bigr) \;\in\; H .$$

**Step 4 (convergence).** Now that $h \in H$, formula (4.2) applies to $h^{(n)} - h \in H$, and
(5.1) reads
$$\bigl\|h^{(n)} - h\bigr\|_H \;\le\; \epsilon \qquad \text{for all } n \ge N(\epsilon) .$$
As $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary and $h$ does not depend on $\epsilon$, this says precisely that
$h^{(n)} \to h$ in $H$.

Thus every Cauchy sequence in $H$ converges to a limit in $H$; that is, $H$ is complete.

## Conclusion

By Sections 2–4, $H = \bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i$ is an inner product space over $\mathbb F$ with
inner product $\langle g,h\rangle_H = \sum_{i\in I}\langle g_i,h_i\rangle_i$, and by Section 5 it
is complete with respect to the induced norm
$\|h\|_H = \bigl(\sum_{i\in I}\|h_i\|_i^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Hence $H$ is a Hilbert space.
$\blacksquare$

## 6. Two remarks

**Remark 6.1 (degenerate cases).** If $I = \varnothing$, then $\prod_{i\in I}H_i$ is a singleton
(the empty family), all sums are $0$, and $H$ is the zero Hilbert space; the argument above covers
this case without change. If $I$ is finite, all summability conditions are vacuous and $H$ is the
usual finite direct sum $H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_n$ with
$\langle g,h\rangle_H = \sum_{k=1}^n\langle g_k,h_k\rangle_k$.

**Remark 6.2 (agreement with the "completion" definition).** Let
$$H_{\mathrm{alg}} := \Bigl\{\,h\in\prod_{i\in I}H_i \;:\; h_i = 0 \text{ for all but finitely many } i\,\Bigr\}$$
be the algebraic direct sum, which is clearly contained in $H$ (all but finitely many partial-sum
terms vanish). Then $H_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is dense in $H$. Indeed, let $h \in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. By
(4.1) there is $F \in \mathcal F(I)$ with $\sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 > \|h\|_H^2 - \epsilon^2$.
Define $h^F \in H_{\mathrm{alg}}$ by $h^F_i := h_i$ for $i \in F$ and $h^F_i := 0$ otherwise. Then
$h - h^F \in H$ has $i$-th entry $0$ for $i \in F$ and $h_i$ for $i \notin F$, so for any
$G\in\mathcal F(I)$,
$$\sum_{i\in G}\|(h-h^F)_i\|_i^2 \;=\; \sum_{i\in G\setminus F}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;=\; \sum_{i\in G\cup F}\|h_i\|_i^2 - \sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;\le\; \|h\|_H^2 - \sum_{i\in F}\|h_i\|_i^2 \;<\; \epsilon^2 ,$$
using (4.3) for the last inequality. Taking the supremum over $G$ gives
$\|h - h^F\|_H \le \epsilon$. Hence $H$ is a complete inner product space containing
$H_{\mathrm{alg}}$ as a dense subspace whose inner product restricts to the natural one on
$H_{\mathrm{alg}}$, i.e. $H$ *is* a completion of the algebraic direct sum. Consequently the
theorem is equally valid under that alternative definition of $\bigoplus_{i\in I}H_i$ (completions
being unique up to isometric isomorphism fixing the dense subspace).
